item.instruction: Write a dialogue describing a phone call between a parent named June Smith and her daughter's doctors office making an appointment for a sports physical. The daughter is named May, she plays soccer, and the doctor's schedule is very busy at the start of the school year.
item.reference: Dr's Office: Hello, this is Dr. Marshall's office, how can I help you? June: Hi, this is June Smith, and I'm calling to make an appointment for my daughter May. Dr's Office: Okay, what type of appointment is this? June: She needs a sports physical for her school soccer team Dr's Office: Sounds good, Dr. Marshall has an appointment available in two weeks on Friday at 10 am June: Is there anyway to see the doctor before then? Dr's Office: Unfortunately, with school starting the schedule is very packed, so that is the first available appointment. June: Okay, I'll take the appointment on the Friday then. See you then! Dr's Office: Sounds good, I'll put you in the schedule. Is there anything else I can help with? June: Nope, that's all. Have a nice day!

Good morning, everyone, and welcome to our All Hands meeting. Today, we’re going to discuss an important topic that affects all of us: our IPO and the upcoming quiet period. As we move closer to this major milestone, it’s essential that we align on what’s ahead and how each of us can contribute to a successful outcome.

Our IPO represents a significant step in our company’s journey. It’s a testament to the hard work, innovation, and dedication of every team member. This is a moment we’ve all worked toward, and it’s a proud day for our company. However, with this opportunity comes a set of responsibilities, especially during the quiet period.

The quiet period is a regulatory requirement that begins when we file our S-1 registration statement with the SEC and continues until 25 days after our IPO. During this time, we must be extremely careful with our communications. Any public statements about our company, financials, or future performance could be misinterpreted or violate securities laws. This includes not only formal press releases but also informal conversations, social media posts, and even casual remarks at events.

Each of you plays a critical role in maintaining the integrity of our messaging during this time. If you’re asked about our financial performance, stock price, or future plans, you should direct the question to our Investor Relations or Legal teams. We have prepared talking points and guidelines to help you navigate these conversations. It’s important to remember that even well-intentioned comments can have unintended consequences.

We also need to be mindful of our internal communications. While we encourage open dialogue and collaboration, we must avoid sharing non-public information, including financial results, product roadmaps, or strategic plans. This includes emails, Slack messages, and in-person discussions. If you have questions or need information, please reach out to the appropriate team or use our internal channels for clarity.

As we prepare for the IPO, we’re also focused on ensuring that our employees are equipped with the knowledge and tools they need to support this transition. We’ll be hosting additional training sessions and Q&A forums in the coming weeks. These will cover everything from investor relations to compliance and communication best practices.

Finally, I want to thank each of you for your continued hard work and commitment. The success of our IPO depends not only on our leadership and financial teams but on every employee who upholds our values and adheres to our guidelines. Let’s work together to ensure a smooth and successful IPO process.

item.instruction: Write me a script for an upcoming All Hands meeting about our IPO prospects and how employees need to act in the quiet period.
item.reference: Lately, I've received plenty of questions about a potential IPO. I want to answer those questions today — and talk about how we as a company will answer questions like that moving forward. For years, we’ve shared that one of our aspirations is to build a wildly successful public company. Everyone has a role to play in getting us there and delivering for customers and growing the business is the most important thing most of us can do. A typical milestone on a high-growth journey is an IPO. But as companies get more serious about a potential IPO, there is a period where they stop talking about an IPO. This might be counter-intuitive, but here’s why: there are important regulatory restrictions on what companies can and cannot say when it comes to company growth and plans as they approach becoming a public company. The consequences if you don’t follow those rules can be serious — the SEC can even delay our ability to go public if it determines we’ve improperly promoted an IPO. And that’s obviously a situation we want to avoid, should we be in a position to go public in the future. And even language like this — "should we be in a position to go public in the future" — is vague. That's for a reason: as we get closer to an IPO, what we can say is restricted and we need to make sure we don’t make promises, otherwise regulators could force us to delay our plans. So I’m going to share some updates about how we’ll need to communicate related to a potential IPO: In order to preserve the ability to IPO at some point in the future, the executive team and I will not be sharing explicit details on our IPO journey or timing at All Hands or in other company communications. We also won’t be sharing updates to our market valuation. Hiring managers and recruiters should not explicitly talk about an IPO or our revenue growth with candidates. Instead, emphasize our massive opportunity, how we’re innovating, delivering value to our customers, and what an awesome team we have. We can’t engage with public market investors or financial journalists on certain topics. That means if a financial analyst, research analyst or reporter reaches out to you, don’t respond and forward the email to the communications team. We also can’t talk about a potential IPO on social media or with friends and family. You get the idea. I know that this will be different for us. We’ve always been a transparent company and this change is hopefully a short-term one. But it is an important one and you all have a role to play in helping us remain compliant. We all have different, important roles to play in making this company a successful, long-term business. The most important thing we can all do is to continue delivering for our customers and building a successful business.

I am writing to express my interest in joining Hats4U as part of your innovative team. As someone with a deep passion for hats and a background in niche technology sales, I believe I can contribute meaningfully to your mission of helping consumers find the perfect hat based on their unique head measurements.

My background in selling specialized technology solutions has equipped me with the skills to engage with clients, understand their needs, and deliver tailored results. I have a proven track record of driving growth in niche markets, and I am excited about the opportunity to apply these skills to a company as forward-thinking as Hats4U.

Hats4U is at the forefront of a unique intersection between fashion and technology, and I am eager to be part of a company that is redefining how consumers interact with personal style. I admire how your company combines precision with personalization, and I am confident that my enthusiasm for hats and my sales expertise align perfectly with your goals.

I am particularly drawn to the way Hats4U leverages technology to solve a common yet overlooked problem. I believe my ability to connect with customers and my understanding of niche markets will allow me to contribute effectively to your continued success.

Thank you for considering my application. I would welcome the opportunity to discuss how my background and passion can support the growth and mission of Hats4U. I look forward to the possibility of working with you.

I have been a huge fan of Hats4U for many years because it's not an exaggeration to say your company changed my life. Spots: Woof, woof! Squeaky toys? I love ‘em, oh yes, I do! Do you have one? Let’s play! Interviewer: Now, now. Sorry Spots, I don’t have a squeaky toy on me at the moment, but we can play later. What is it about squeaky toys do you love so much? Spots: What else is there to love but the squeak? I love, love, love those sweet squeaks! It’s music to my floppy ears, and I feel like a big scary wolf. Interviewer: So the squeaking is appealing to your hunting instincts? Spots: Woof! Yes! Then I tear a hole in it, and my human has to take it away, and I am sad. Interviewer: Oh, no. Well, they do that so you don’t hurt yourself. Your human gets you a new one, right? Spots: Yes, yes! I’m never without a squeaky toy for long! *smiles and pants* Interviewer: Well, that wraps up our interview. Thank you for joining us, Spots! Spots: Thank you! Woof! Interview: Good boy!

As a critic with a discerning eye for children’s literature, I found the narrative predictable and the moralizing heavy-handed. The Lorax himself, though charming in concept, lacks the depth required to engage more thoughtful young minds. Dr. Seuss’s rhyming style, while playful, often sacrifices clarity for rhythm, resulting in a text that feels more like a recitation than a story. The illustrations, though colorful, are derivative of the author’s earlier works and offer little in the way of innovation. While *The Lorax* may serve as a gentle introduction to ecological themes for the youngest of children, it does little to challenge or inspire. For a critic who values both substance and style in children’s books, *The Lorax* is a modest, if not forgettable, entry in the genre.

item.reference: Billy shifted around, peeking out at the doorway from underneath his bed. He still sniffled, sometimes wiping his arm across his nose. Maybe if he waited long enough, they'd just forget about it, and he could come out? His heart raced as he heard his dad climbing the stairs, his large boots appearing in the doorframe. He heard a loud sigh and cringed a bit as his dad walked over to his bed and sat, the mattress sinking under his weight and nearly brushing against his head. "Bill..." His hands clenched at his dad's voice. "It's okay, honestly. We know it was an accident. Why are you so scared?" Seconds passed, and the child's voice rose up from under the bed. "It was your dad's. And I know you loved it, so I wanted to see it, and I didn't think I'd drop it and..." Dan heard his son's small voice crack. "And I'm sorry." His heart broke to hear how sad his son was. The frame with his father's medals was salvageable, if a bit scuffed. The glass was not, obviously, but that could always be replaced. "It's fine. We can fix it." "...really?" "Yeah, but that's not what's important. I want you to know that no matter what, you never have to be scared of us or what we'll say or do." He patted the bed. "Come on, Bill." His son slowly appeared from under the bed, eyes, and nose red and slick with tears. He still seemed mortified. Dan wrapped him up in a great big hug. "See? Even if you do something wrong, you might end up getting punished, but we're always to love you, no matter what. And this wasn't even something wrong. You just made a mistake. That's all." He wiped the tears from his son's eyes and ruffled his hair. "Mostly, I was just worried that you could hurt yourself by grabbing that. It's pretty big, huh?" "Yeah, I thought I could hold it, but it was so heavy and..." He laughed, hugging him again. "It's okay. Tell you what, we'll go get it fixed together tomorrow. Now go wash your face. We'll go get dinner." He sighed in relief as his son trotted off. Wait until Anna hears about this.

Every night, the bell rang. It started as a faint echo, barely perceptible through the thick forest that surrounded the house. I had rented this remote cabin to finish my third novel, hoping the silence would help me focus. But the sound grew louder each evening, as if the bell were drawing closer, determined to be heard.

The house was old, built into the side of a hill, with creaking floorboards and a single window that overlooked the valley. I had chosen it for its isolation, but now I wondered if I had chosen it for another reason. The bell was never the same twice. Sometimes it was a deep, resonant chime, other times a sharp, metallic clang. It always came from the direction of the mountain, but the distance between the sound and the house seemed to shrink each night.

I tried to ignore it, to focus on the novel. I wrote for hours, only to find my thoughts drifting back to the bell. It was as if the sound was a character in my story, one that refused to be ignored. I began to write about it, weaving it into the plot of my novel. The protagonist heard the same bell, and with each passing night, it grew louder, drawing them toward an unknown fate.

One night, I could no longer stand the silence between the rings. I packed a flashlight and a notebook and ventured out into the forest. The air was thick with mist, and the path was nearly invisible. I followed the sound, step by step, until I reached the edge of a cliff. There, nestled in the rocks, was a small bell, rusted and worn. I touched it, and it rang out, louder than ever.

I returned to the house, shaken. The bell was real, but why had it drawn me here? I sat at my desk, staring at the blank page. The novel was no longer just a story—it was a reflection of my own journey. Every night, the bell rang, louder and closer, as if urging me to finish what I had started. I picked up my pen and wrote, not for the world, but for the sound that had followed me to this remote house, ringing every night, louder with each passing evening.

item.reference: *Lauren's face was filled with fear. Would they make it on time? Suddenly-* *Ding, ding, ding! * " Forget it!" I yelled, slamming my pencil down on the table. My notebook nearly slid off of it. " That stupid bell!" I looked out a nearby window. The sun was setting between the snow-topped pine trees which surrounded the little glade my house was in. I ruffled my hair and sighed. I glanced at the clock above the doorway to the bedroom. Yep, 8:30 exactly. Picking up the pencil, I stared into the page of the notebook I was on. Nothing came to me. For two weeks, I had been hearing this bell. Every night at exactly 6:30. Now, I am not going to try explaining this to you, for the very good reason that I can't. It was not a church bell, and even if it would be, I lived in a cottage way out in the middle of nowhere. But the weird thing was, it got louder and louder every night... I took a sip of coffee and continued writing for a bit. But it was really unsuccessful. I had a lot of erasing and ripping out pages. *I should really get a laptop, * I thought. Then, I got on a really good roll again with my novel when- *Ding, ding, ding! * A second time? This hadn't happened before... I put my pencil down again. I looked around the room I was in, not really sure what I was looking for. Then, the lights turned off. *Ding, ding, ding! * " Oh gosh!" I yelled. A hideous voice from very nearby said, " Yes, oh gosh. Why haven't you come when I have called? Why, you are just a little wretched old fellow!" A bony hand gripped me and put me on the floor. " Aah!" I yelled. Two eyes glowed in the dark. " Who are you? Get out of my house!!!!" " Relax! This is not your house. It's mine! Now won't you please wake up, darling!" *Ding, ding, ding! * I woke with a start. My mother was there. " What's all the fuss, honey? Go back to bed, it's 3 am."

item.instruction: Write a letter to Dear Abby on relationship advice.
item.reference: Dear Abby, I hope this letter finds you well. I am writing to seek your advice as my relationship with my partner has gotten to an unbearable stage in the last few weeks and is weighing heavy on my mind. We have been together for seventeen years now. We love each other deeply but have been struggling to connect on a deeper level. I want this relationship to work more than anything in the world, but I am unsure where to start. I have tried talking to him about my feelings, but he seems to shrug me off at any attempt. It feels like the rock has set in.I look forward to hearing your thoughts. Sincerely, Mrs. Mavis.

rounds.text: He stumbled upon the partially built treehouse nestled in the crook of an old oak, its wooden frame jutting awkwardly from the trunk. Vines curled around the unfinished planks, as if nature itself had tried to reclaim the structure. Curious, he climbed the ladder, his boots creaking against the splintered wood. Inside, a single chair sat beneath a makeshift window, and a half-finished sketch of a starry sky lay on the floor. It was clear someone had started something special but never finished. He ran his fingers over the rough edges, imagining the laughter it might have held. A breeze rustled through the leaves, whispering secrets of the past. He sat in the chair, gazing out at the horizon, and for the first time in years, felt a spark of hope. Maybe he would finish what someone else had begun.

item.instruction: Write a short story about a man who discovers a partially built treehouse.
item.reference: A man purchased a piece of property and began to explore the land. After some time had passed, the man discovered a partially built treehouse not too far from the ground that would be safe for his children to play in. The man returned home to his workshop to gather wood and tools to complete the treehouse construction. However, upon arrival at his workshop, he learned that he would need more wood to finish the treehouse. Disappointed, he began to put his tools away when he heard a truck passing by with lumber for sale. After purchasing the material, he returned to the treehouse with his tools and material and began to work. Upon completion of the treehouse, he called for his children to surprise them and when they saw the treehouse they shouted for joy and immediately began to play in it and this made the man very happy.

item.instruction: Write a letter to a home seller named Ms Johnson explaining why we are interested in purchasing her home. We are a person from Washington and a person from Colorado. Focus on the natural beauty of the home, the location, and the extra space for pottery and woodworking.
item.reference: Dear Ms. Johnson, We recently made the decision to relocate and feel that your property will be the perfect place for us to begin our new chapter. It is clear to see the care and attention you have put into expanding and maintaining this home over the years and we look forward to continuing to do the same as homeowners. I am originally from Washington, and my partner is from Colorado. We met in college and have grown our life out of state together for the past twelve years. The last two years have given us more flexibility and helped us realize that what is most important to us is building a home together where we feel safe and close to family, but also inspired and fulfilled. We feel that is exactly what your home will bring to our lives. The unique, natural design of the house and the stunning and spacious lot provide both an immediately comfortable home with room to grow over the years. We look forward to building out the garage with a woodworking shop, setting up the artist shed on the river as a pottery studio, cooking meals for friends and family in the wonderful kitchen, and finding a perfect spot in the yard for a vegetable garden. We want to care and tend this home much as you have for the years you have lived here, and we sincerely appreciate being considered as the next owners of this beautiful property.

Where imaginary friends come out to stay.  
There’s a monster, fierce with eyes of flame,

item.instruction: Write a poem for a 12 years old child that visualizes the imaginary friends of a small child. It could rhyme and show the physicality of those imaginary friends. Depict the moods of each child. One friend is an angry monster. One is a small thing like asparagus who has big toes. A giant Broccoli is another friend who’s almost as big as this child. The child’s name is Devon.
item.reference: In the mind of Devon, a world full of wonder, Where imaginary friends play and never sunder, A monster with fangs and eyes all aglow, Growls and grunts, his anger on show. A small thing, like an asparagus with toes so big, Giggles and jumps, like a lively whirling twig, Dancing and prancing, never still or tame, With an odd personality, but never the same. Then comes the giant broccoli, so tall and grand, Almost as big as Devon, so mighty it stands, Although big and strong, this friend is full of grace, His face is like a smile and heart, solace. They all are unique no matter the place, They play all day with smiles on their face, Their moods were so lively, their colors so bright, His imaginary friends are a beautiful sight. So let Devon play on with his imaginary band, And let his friends lead him to an enchanted land, For in their safe embrace, the child will always find, A world full of wonder, where friendships intertwine.

I began as a cucumber, green and plump, nestled among my siblings in the field. The sun kissed my skin, and the earth cradled me in its warm embrace. I was young, full of life, and unaware of the journey that awaited me. The farmers tended to us with care, watering us, protecting us from the elements. I grew, stretching toward the sky, dreaming of nothing more than becoming a part of the harvest.

One morning, I was plucked from the field, my roots severed, my life uprooted. I was taken to a cool, dimly lit room where I was scrubbed and cleaned, my skin polished until it gleamed. I was no longer a cucumber, but I was still whole, still unbroken. The air smelled of vinegar and salt, and I felt a strange tingling in my skin as I was submerged in a briny bath. The world around me shifted, and I began to change.

Days passed, and I transformed. My green hue deepened, turning into a rich, golden hue. My once-tender flesh grew firm, and I took on a new identity—pickle. I was no longer just a vegetable; I was preserved, ready to be enjoyed in sandwiches, on salads, or in the quiet comfort of a jar. I was no longer in the field, but I was still alive in a different way.

I was placed into a jar, nestled among my fellow pickles, each of us a product of the same transformation. The lid was sealed, and I was stored away, waiting for the day when someone would open me and bring me back to life. I was content in my new home, knowing that I had been given a second chance, a new purpose.

The seasons changed, and the world outside the jar moved on. But I remained, preserved in time, a memory of the field, a testament to the journey from cucumber to pickle. I was no longer just a vegetable, but a symbol of change, of preservation, of the quiet magic that happens when nature meets human hands.

And though I would never see the field again, I carried its essence within me, a piece of the earth that had once cradled me. I was a pickle, born from a cucumber, shaped by the field, and now forever sealed in a jar, waiting for my moment to shine once more.

item.instruction: Write a story from the perspective of a pickle as it is going from a cucumber in the field to being jarred and put away for the year.
item.reference: I am a pickle. Well, no that isn't quite right, I'm a cucumber right now but soon I will be a pickle. Days ago some friendly hands picked me up from my nice sunny patch in the field. I was about ready to come in, to be honest, the heat was getting to me and there were far too many rabbits lurking around. It was very nice to be carried inside, given a nice cool bath, and set aside for the night to sleep and relax. I woke up a bit later than usual still surrounded in the colander by my other cucumber friends. They were still sleeping so I did my best not to disturb them. They weren't a talkative bunch normally anyway. The sun was just starting to peak in through the curtains above the sink when a lady entered the room. The same lady who grabbed me from the patch yesterday. She seemed very friendly and nice. At least I thought so until she picked me up, bowl and all, and gave me a big shake. What a way to rise and shine. I could hear the other cucumbers grumbling too. She transported us a few feet away to another part of the countertop. Then, the lady mixed a bunch of ingredients in a big pot on the stove and it started to smell good but it also tickled my nose a bit. Perhaps a bit too garlicky for my tastes. Next thing I knew she was picking me up again but this time she stuck me in a jar! I couldn't believe it, it was finally happening! It's the most exciting day in any gherkins life. A few of my other cucumber friends joined me and we all nestled up close to each other. It was very cozy and everyone had a nice view through the glass too. Then, the nice lady gave us a warm bath. It felt even nicer than the cool bath I had before. It had hints of dill and pepper and it covered me from my tippy toes all the way to the top of my head. She put a nice little roof over top sealing me in. And I knew that from this day forward I was a cucumber no more, now I was one proud pickle.

The office was a cathedral of fluorescent light and sterile silence, its walls lined with the same beige panels that had stood for decades. Every morning, he trudged through the same routine—coffee from the machine that never brewed properly, a stale muffin from the vending machine, and the same spreadsheet that never seemed to finish updating. His days blurred into one another, each filled with the same monotony, the same deadlines, the same unspoken expectation that he would endure. He had long since stopped caring about the work itself; it was the lifestyle that had become a prison, a cycle of obligation and exhaustion that left no room for anything else.

He sat at his desk, fingers numb from the keyboard, eyes burning from the screen. The clock on the wall ticked forward, each second a reminder of how little time he had left before the next meeting, the next report, the next demand. His colleagues were no different, all of them trapped in the same invisible web, their faces pale and tired, their laughter hollow. There was no escape, no reprieve, only the relentless march of the workday.

He had once dreamed of something more—of travel, of art, of a life that didn’t revolve around spreadsheets and performance reviews. But those dreams had been buried beneath the weight of rent, bills, and the unspoken fear of failure. He had no savings, no skills, no plan. Just the office, the routine, and the slow erosion of his own spirit.

At night, he would collapse onto his small bed, the city’s lights flickering through the window like distant stars. He would stare at the ceiling, wondering if this was all there was—this endless cycle of work and sleep, of obligation and resignation. The thought of quitting was there, always, but it was a whisper, drowned out by the noise of the world outside.

One evening, as he left the office, he noticed a figure standing near the entrance, watching him. The man was older, his posture hunched, his face lined with the weight of years. He didn’t look like anyone from the office, yet something about him felt familiar, as if he had been waiting for him, or perhaps, had once been him.

item.instruction: I want you to write a narrative with a bleak, depressing tone about an office worker who is overworked and dislikes his lifestyle. Give me more than 300 words. Make it third person. Don't include dialogue. Introduce another character right at the end.
item.reference: Maurice walked home in the dark after work. He'd been up since before the sun had risen and was stuck in the office the entire day. His only chance to see the sunlight was on a trip between office floors. He'd gotten to bask in the sun for a few minutes while waiting for the elevator. As he shuffled down the street heading home, he wondered how long it would keep up. He had been single since graduating high school. He started working right out of college. He had been promoted once, but even with all his money life didn't seem any brighter. What was there to spend the money on? He stopped by a Mcdonald's on the way home and grabbed something for dinner. The night shift recognized him. They chatted a bit while he waited for his food, but it made him feel worse. How often had he gone there at night? How many times did he have to go there for them to have become accustomed to him? He ate his fries out of the bag on his way home but stopped in a park and finished his food on the bench there. He couldn't bring himself to take the food home. What was the point in living this lifestyle where work consumed his life, and no one waited for him at home? Something had to change, and it needed to change soon. He could go drinking, but drinking alone was worse than just going home. He could go to a girl's bar, of course, and be surrounded by beautiful women while drinking and venting his troubles. However, it was just a job to them. They didn't care one bit about his problems or who he was. Maurice sighed and stared at the moon for a time before a woman entered the park, sitting on the swing and crying.

item.instruction: I'm an English speaker trying to learn Japanese Kanji using mnemonics. Mnemonics for Kanji are created from the primitives that make them up. The Kanji for Tax has the primitives wheat and devil, so an example would be, "Taxes are like the devil taking away your hard earned wheat". Can you create a mnemonic for the Kanji meaning Wish that has the primitives clock and heart?
item.reference: Sure! How about, "A wish from the heart beats like the ticking of a clock, reminding us to never give up hope."

rounds.text: No formula generates all prime numbers deterministically. Prime numbers follow patterns but are not truly random. Their distribution appears irregular, yet mathematical models like the Prime Number Theorem describe their density. While no simple formula exists, algorithms and sieves can identify primes. The randomness of primes is a subject of ongoing research, with conjectures like the Riemann Hypothesis aiming to explain their distribution more precisely. Thus, primes are not truly random but follow complex, non-random rules.

item.instruction: Can we find a formula to generate all prime numbers, and is the distribution of primes truly random?
item.reference: There are several formulas that generate all prime numbers, but they're not efficient enough to be of any practical use. For example, a formula devised by C. P. Willans in 1964 does technically return the $n$th prime, but it does so by summing $2^n$ values, each of which requires a factorial to compute. As for randomness, as the set of prime numbers is fixed, it can't be "truly" random, only pseudorandom. It's also not uniform, as evidenced by e.g. the Ulam spiral and its unnatural frequency of straight lines.

The valley of madness had been his home for too long, but now he sought something more. His acquaintance listened, sensing the depth of his turmoil. Stumbling through the dimly lit corridors of Tegra Corp, the sudden darkness was disorienting. The emergency lights flickered to life, casting an eerie glow across the concrete walls and the scattered remnants of a failed power grid. You had no idea how long you had been wandering, only that the building’s systems had gone dark without warning. Now, as the emergency lights pulsed with a steady, artificial glow, you found yourself standing before a massive vault door, its surface cold and unyielding.

The door began to grind open, a low, mechanical groan echoing through the chamber. You stepped forward, heart pounding, as the massive steel barrier slowly parted, revealing a room lined with servers, data drives, and the unmistakable hum of stored information. This was no ordinary storage room—it was the heart of Tegra’s most sensitive operations. The vault was a fortress of digital security, and now, it was yours to explore.

As you entered, the emergency lights bathed the room in a pale blue hue, illuminating rows of encrypted drives and blinking status indicators. You could feel the weight of the moment pressing down on you. This was the kind of place that required clearance levels higher than your own, yet here you were, an intern, standing in the center of it all. The power failure had left the building in chaos, and now, with the vault door open, you had a rare opportunity to see what Tegra was truly hiding.

You moved cautiously, scanning the room for anything out of place. The emergency lights flickered again, casting long shadows across the floor. Somewhere in the distance, the hum of the building’s backup generators could be heard, a low, steady sound that suggested the power might be returning soon. You had to act fast.

Your eyes landed on a terminal near the center of the room, its screen dark. You reached out, fingers trembling slightly, and pressed the power button. The screen flickered to life, displaying a login prompt. You hesitated for a moment, then typed in the credentials you had seen in a restricted document earlier that day. The screen blinked, and a message appeared: “Access Granted.”

The vault was open, and so was the door to Tegra’s secrets. You had stumbled into something far bigger than you had ever imagined, and now, with the emergency lights still glowing and the vault door wide open, you had to decide what to do next.

item.instruction: A new engineering intern at Tegra Corp, you find yourself stumbling blindly through the hallways after a massive power failure. When the emergency lights glow, you are in a room with a massive vault. The door starts to grind open.
item.reference: A dull rumble vibrated the floor beneath my feet, and I could feel something happening. *Finally*. The lights had been out for almost an hour, and I had been in one of the most remote segments of the facility dropping off a package for Dr. Horz, one of the biotech R & D gurus. I had been stumbling around for what felt like ages, but my watch did confirm that it was only 56 minutes. *56 minutes of noiseless terror*. This particular R & D facility of Tegra was filled with wonders, but it was very nearly empty. I was in my second week of interning, a lowly, aspiring electrical engineer. Thus far, I had done little more than grunt work with the odd bit of logic design. Mostly just documentation though. Endless documentation. The ground stopped trembling, and the lights slowly inked a light incandescence. The walls in front of me slowly illuminated, and I was peering at a tremendous vault. A vault door—to be specific. A vault door…which was slightly cracked open. The metallic alloy comprising its structure wasn ’ t flush with the surrounding wall. And then the door started cracking open more. The noise was probably the most frightening thing. The grinding of gears and servos, attempting to hold the door shut, was echoing riotously throughout the small room. I started backing away slowly. I don ’ t know where I am. I don ’ t know what is behind that door, and I don ’ t want to be here anymore. I take a large, decisive step towards the door, and I hear a different kind of rumble—a throaty rumble, from some *thing*. And then the door quite literally gave up its effort to hold whatever was within and sprang backwards, slamming into the wall. The darkness was wholly shrouding the space beyond. A deep, primal terror was creeping into every nook of my being. What the *fuck* is happening? And then I see it. Six or seven feet in the air, slowly apparating into existence as the gentle illumination of the emergency lighting found it. A long, tube, slowly tapering to a point. No, not one. Many. The *presence* became more pronounced in the room. I watched as the objects source grew more visible. Dense, matted hair. The tubes were sprouting from it. And then the eyes. Yellow—slitted—orbs. It sprang. The last thing I perceived in those final moments, as my body was wrapped handily in a clawed grip, was a pronounced and deliberate, “ Meow. ”

Woody didn't get the batteries in the baby monitor quick enough. The moment the door creaked open, Andy and all the birthday guests froze in their tracks. There, on the floor, the toys were huddled together, alive and moving. It was as if time had paused mid-sentence, leaving everyone in stunned silence. The room, once filled with the cheerful sounds of laughter and birthday songs, now echoed with an eerie stillness.

Woody stood frozen, his eyes locked on the scene before him. He had always known the toys came to life when no one was watching, but this was different. This was not the quiet, secret world of the night. This was daylight, and the room was full of people. The realization hit him like a brick. He had failed to act fast enough. He hadn't replaced the batteries in the baby monitor quickly enough, and now the entire world had seen the truth.

Andy's face was a mix of confusion and disbelief. His eyes darted between the toys and Woody, as if trying to make sense of the impossible. The guests, too, were frozen in place, some whispering, others staring wide-eyed. A few had already pulled out their phones, trying to capture the moment, but no one dared to move.

The toys, sensing the sudden attention, began to shift slightly, as if unsure of how to react. Buzz Lightyear stood tall, his helmet slightly askew, while Mr. Potato Head adjusted his eyes with a nervous flick of his fingers. Hamm rolled onto his back, his eyes wide with surprise. The room was a stage, and the toys were the unexpected performers.

Woody took a step forward, his voice breaking the silence. "Everyone, please, just—just stay calm." His words were shaky, but they carried a weight that made the room listen. He turned to Andy, his voice dropping to a whisper. "We need to get them back to the floor, out of sight. Now."

Andy nodded, his mind racing. He looked around at the guests, some of whom were still frozen in place, others beginning to move. "Okay, okay, everyone, just—just stay where you are. Don't move. Don't blink." His voice was firm, but there was a tremor beneath it.

The toys, sensing the urgency, began to shuffle back toward the floor, their movements slow and deliberate. Woody watched them go, his heart pounding. He had failed to act quickly enough, but now, with the help of Andy and the guests, they had a chance to fix the mistake. The floor was their sanctuary, and they would return to it, hidden once more from the world.

He hadn't replaced the batteries in the baby monitor quickly enough, and now the entire world had seen the truth.

Andy's face was a mix of confusion and disbelief. His eyes darted between the toys and Woody, as if trying to make sense of the impossible. The guests, too, were frozen in place, some whispering, others staring wide-eyed. A few had already pulled out their phones, trying to capture the moment, but no one dared to move.

The toys, sensing the sudden attention, began to shift slightly, as if unsure of how to react. Buzz Lightyear stood tall, his helmet slightly askew, while Mr. Potato Head adjusted his eyes with a nervous flick of his fingers. Hamm rolled onto his back, his eyes wide with surprise. The room was a stage, and the toys were the unexpected performers.

Woody took a step forward, his voice breaking the silence. "Everyone, please, just—just stay calm." His words were shaky, but they carried a weight that made the room listen. He turned to Andy, his voice dropping to a whisper. "We need to get them back to the floor, out of sight. Now."

Andy nodded, his mind racing. He looked around at the guests, some of whom were still frozen in place, others beginning to move. "Okay, okay, everyone, just—just stay where you are. Don't move. Don't blink." His voice was firm, but there was a tremor beneath it.

The toys, sensing the urgency, began to shuffle back toward the floor, their movements slow and deliberate. Woody watched them go, his heart pounding. He had failed to act quickly enough, but now, with the help of Andy and the guests, they had a chance to fix the mistake. The floor was their sanctuary, and they would return to it, hidden once more from the world.

item.reference: I looked up in horror at the crowd of young boys came thundering into the room. The clouds on the walls were suddenly blocked by a horde of scrambling young bodies and flailing limbs. I froze, the hat on my head tilted just enough for me to see everything, and i saw fear. Andy stood there in the middle of the floor, clutching the dreaded spaceman box, but that seemed to matter less compared to the pressing matter. The air was still, I could feel Mr.Potato head's round eyes blink and the sound of heavy breathing from the guests penetrated the silence with jagged blades of uncertainty. I considered freezing, but it was too late. We all knew it. Rex panicked like a child who came down christmas morning to find no gifts. He thundered across the hardwood floors for the window, yelling at the top of his lungs some inaudible dinosaur screech. I spun around, knowing it was too late and pointed towards the window. The toys didn't need a second prompt. The strong man and Mr. Potato head grabbed the monkeys in a barrel, hopped in RC and gunned the engines. The army men attempted to rescue some of the less mobile toys, but it was too late. One brilliant child had the idea to grab my waist with his sweaty, greasy hand and hold me up in the air. I put up a fight, hoping to distract them enough to let everyone escape. I didn't know what would happen, but panic had overrun my emotions and pure terror coursed through my plastic veins. But then, salvation. Andy wrenched me from the child's grasp and shouted angrily " YOU ONLY GOT ME BEDSHEETS." He held me gently in his grasp and managed to utter " Woody?" I stared back up at him with and sorrow filled my soul. I knew this was it, the other toys were out. " I'm sorry Andy, you'll understand one day." I flung my sack cloth limbs out of his hand and towards the bed, hitting it with surprising force. I propelled myself towards the window, clear through the slit. The other toys were already at the edge of the law waiting for me, but I had to look back at least once. Andy stared out the window with a look of pure despair on his face and one confused spaceman peered back, blinking quizzically towards the small group of toys, running down the street; never to return.
